required_recommendations: Establish last known well (08:30, about 1 hour 15 minutes before arrival at 09:45; he was well on waking and at work) and the NIHSS (2: limb ataxia 2). His inability to walk without support is not scored and makes the deficit disabling.
Obtain non-contrast CT head FIRST to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before any thrombolytic decision.
Verify glucose to exclude hypoglycemia as a stroke mimic.

Apply HINTS to separate central from peripheral vertigo: a normal head impulse test (no corrective saccade), direction-changing nystagmus or skew deviation each point to a central cause, while a positive head impulse with a corrective saccade is the peripheral pattern. Here the head impulse is normal and the nystagmus changes direction, so HINTS is central despite the absence of skew.

IV thrombolysis: give (about 1 hour 15 minutes from last known well; disabling gait ataxia; CT without hemorrhage; BP 132/81 mmHg; glucose 98 mg/dL, platelets 258, INR 1.1; the left vertebral dissection is extracranial (V3, ending at the dural ring) and is not a contraindication). Thrombectomy: not indicated (no large vessel occlusion; basilar and right vertebral arteries patent).

Give alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (maximum 90 mg) or tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (maximum 25 mg) with a door-to-needle time under 60 minutes; blood pressure needs no lowering beforehand, and keep it below 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after.

Admit to a stroke unit with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry) for at least the first 24 hours, with neurological checks for post-thrombolysis hemorrhage and cerebellar swelling; repeat imaging on any decline.

After imaging at 24 hours excludes hemorrhage, start antithrombotic therapy for the extracranial vertebral dissection for at least 3 months: clopidogrel 75 mg daily, because he is allergic to aspirin (urticaria), or anticoagulation (AHA/ASA 2021 secondary prevention, COR 2a; CADISS).
Stop sumatriptan (triptans are contraindicated after ischemic stroke) and avoid ibuprofen during antithrombotic therapy; use acetaminophen and review his migraine treatment.

Do not refer for PFO closure now: the stroke has a determined cause, the left vertebral dissection, and the closure trials and the AAN 2020 advisory concern strokes without another mechanism; record the PFO with atrial septal aneurysm for follow-up.
Repeat non-invasive vessel imaging (CTA or MRA) at 3 to 6 months to assess healing and decide the duration of antithrombotic therapy; advise avoiding neck strain, such as rock climbing, until then.

Start atorvastatin 80 mg daily: LDL 117 mg/dL after a non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke without known coronary disease meets the AHA/ASA 2021 secondary prevention indication (COR 1, SPARCL), although the mechanism is the vertebral dissection rather than atherosclerosis; target LDL below 70 mg/dL.

key_clinical_evidence: Sudden vertigo, vomiting, oscillopsia, left limb ataxia and inability to walk in a 35-year-old is a posterior circulation syndrome until proven otherwise; CT first excludes cerebellar hemorrhage.
HINTS is central: normal head impulse (no corrective saccade) and direction-changing nystagmus; the absence of skew does not make it peripheral, because any one central sign is enough (Kattah 2009).
NIHSS is 2 (limb ataxia 2); gaze is 0, since nystagmus and saccadic pursuit do not score. Gait ataxia is not scored, so the low score understates a disabling deficit.

Left neck soreness during a long cycling ride 3 days earlier is the prodrome of a left vertebral artery dissection; the T1-hyperintense intramural hematoma on fat-saturated MRI fits a dissection about 3 days old, with a hyperacute infarct.

IV thrombolysis is given: about 1 hour 15 minutes from last known well, disabling deficit, no hemorrhage, normal glucose, platelets and INR. The dissection is extracranial (V3, ending at the dural ring), which is not a contraindication; there is no large vessel occlusion, so no thrombectomy.

The known PFO with atrial septal aneurysm is incidental: the ipsilateral vertebral dissection is a determined cause, so the stroke is not cryptogenic and PFO closure is not indicated (AAN 2020; the closure trials enrolled cryptogenic strokes only).
Thrombophilia testing is not indicated: the mechanism is arterial dissection, and his father's deep vein thrombosis is a venous event.

For extracranial cervical artery dissection, antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for at least 3 months is reasonable (AHA/ASA 2021, COR 2a); his aspirin allergy makes clopidogrel the antiplatelet choice.
Sumatriptan is contraindicated after ischemic stroke and must be stopped; ibuprofen adds bleeding risk on antithrombotic therapy.
Only glucose had to be known before thrombolysis here (no anticoagulant, no suspected coagulopathy); ECG and troponin do not delay reperfusion, and CTA does not wait for creatinine.

clinical_pearls: The HINTS exam outperforms early MRI in the first 24-48 hours for detecting central causes of acute vestibular syndrome; a normal head impulse test or direction-changing nystagmus alone indicates a central cause
Vertebral artery dissection is a leading cause of posterior circulation stroke in patients under 45 and is frequently preceded by neck pain, minor cervical trauma or sustained neck extension
A PFO, even with an atrial septal aneurysm, is set aside when another mechanism such as an ipsilateral arterial dissection explains the stroke; closure evidence applies to cryptogenic stroke
Posterior fossa infarcts can progress to cerebellar edema with brainstem compression and hydrocephalus, requiring monitoring and potential neurosurgical decompression

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Carlos Reyes is a 35-year-old right-handed man with a history of episodic migraines and an incidentally discovered patent foramen ovale who presents to the emergency department via private vehicle with his girlfriend at approximately 09:45 this morning complaining of sudden onset severe vertigo, nausea, and vomiting. The patient reports that he woke up at 07:00 feeling entirely well and went to work as usual. At approximately 08:30, while sitting at his desk, he experienced an abrupt onset of intense room-spinning dizziness accompanied by severe nausea. He attempted to stand and immediately veered to the left, nearly falling into his desk. He vomited twice within the first fifteen minutes. He also noticed that objects appeared to be moving and jumping, worse when looking to the left. He denies any hearing loss, tinnitus, ear fullness, or aural pressure. There was no headache at onset, although he now reports a mild occipital discomfort that he attributes to the sustained vomiting. He denies any limb weakness, numbness, or tingling. He reports no recent upper respiratory infection, viral illness, or ear symptoms in the preceding weeks. His girlfriend, who drove him to the ED, reports that his speech sounds normal and he has been fully coherent throughout, though he appears extremely unsteady and has been unable to walk without support. The emergency physician on initial evaluation noted that the patient appeared to have a peripheral vestibular syndrome and considered vestibular neuritis as the leading diagnosis. However, the patient's young age, sudden onset at rest, and presence of a known PFO prompted neurology consultation. On further questioning, the patient reports that approximately three days ago he went on a long cycling ride during which he experienced a transient episode of neck soreness on the left side, which he attributed to positioning on the bike. He did not seek medical attention for this.
